ideas.title: Where the day-10 error actually lives - and why it is not mostly polar
ideas.verdict: Claim under test: the polar cap dominates day-10 error, so fixing the graph at the poles is the largest available win. Assessment: PARTLY WRONG, and the correction matters for what to build next. An earlier reading of the year-mean bias maps put ~55% of day-10 area-weighted squared MSL error poleward of 60 degrees. That figure is the SYSTEMATIC BIAS budget, not the RMSE budget. Measured properly with scripts/evaluate_zone_rmse_dominance.py on both best 2.5 degree models, the poleward-of-60 share of day-10 area-weighted squared error is 32.4% for z500, 33.8% for msl, 43.0% for t2m and only 2.2% for q700 - over-represented against a 13.4% area share, but nowhere near a majority. The single largest band is the Southern Ocean storm track 60S-45S at 25.0% of z500 error on 7.9% of area. Decisive scoping fact: the bands where the lat-lon graph is worst are NOT the bands holding the error. Where the graph is severely degraded (|lat|>75, edges 2.70x shorter than at the equator) sits 7.3% of z500 error; where the most error sits (|lat| 45-60, 41.9%) the graph is only 1.23x degraded. Graph work is therefore worth doing but has a bounded ceiling, and it is not the biggest lever visible in this measurement. The biggest is a separate defect this run exposed: t2m is WORSE THAN PERSISTENCE at day 10 over the tropics and the Southern Ocean.

sections.heading: Evidence 1 - day-10 share of area-weighted squared error poleward of 60 degrees (both best models; zone_rmse_dominance_summary.csv)

blocks.text: The two models agree to within 1.5 points on every variable. Capacity does not change WHERE the error lives - consistent with the separate finding that +55% width and a doubled S1 base left the polar share unmoved. q700 is the outlier in the other direction: moisture error is tropical, so a polar fix does nothing for it.

sections.heading: Evidence 2 - z500 day 10 by zone, h160 (share, over-representation, and skill vs persistence)

blocks.text: Read the last two columns together. The 60S-45S band carries the most error of any zone, but its skill against persistence (0.556) is among the BETTER scores in the table - the error is large there because the weather is large, not because the model is weak. The genuinely weak non-tropical zone is 75N-90N: 2.44x over-represented AND the lowest z500 skill outside the tropics (0.485). That Arctic cell is the clean model-weakness signal, and it is 4.2% of the budget.

sections.heading: Evidence 3 - the graph is worst exactly where the error is not (L0 of graph_2p5_k8_l3k24_hybrid_row_aware_L3_v4.pt, measured directly)

blocks.text: This is the table that should decide the graph roadmap. Degradation and error concentration are anti-correlated over the range that matters: the band holding 41.9% of z500 day-10 error is only 1.23x degraded, while the 2.70x-degraded band holds 7.3%. A fix that only reaches the true polar caps addresses at most 7.3% of the budget.

items: Confirmed independently from the graph file: 288 pole-row nodes emit 2016 L0 edges and ZERO of them join the north pole row to the south pole row. Within the north pole row the largest longitude separation spanned by any edge is 7.5 degrees - a genuine over-the-pole link would join points about 180 degrees apart. There is no path over either pole.
L3 (the coarsest level, 162 nodes) reaches a maximum |lat| of exactly 80.00 degrees and has ZERO nodes poleward of 80 - the caps lose coarse-scale coverage entirely.

Upper bounds on what a perfect polar fix buys, from the shares above: eliminating ALL z500 error poleward of 75 degrees would cut global day-10 z500 RMSE by 3.7%; halving all error poleward of 60 degrees would cut it by 8.5%. For msl the same two bounds are 4.1% and 8.8%. These are ceilings, not forecasts.

sections.heading: Evidence 4 - the larger finding: t2m is worse than persistence over ocean

blocks.text: Negative skill means the 10-day forecast is worse than simply holding the initial condition fixed. t2m over the tropical oceans and the Southern Ocean is in that regime. This is the signature of a missing lower boundary condition: over ocean, t2m is essentially SST-driven and nearly constant across 10 days, so persistence is very strong, and a model with no prescribed SST or sea-ice input has nothing to anchor it and drifts. This configuration has extra_features disabled and copies only orography, so no surface boundary field is prescribed forward in time.

items: This is cheap to test relative to any graph change and does not touch the graph at all. The tree already carries a pending suggestion node for known-future forcings.

It also caps what graph work can achieve for t2m specifically: 43% of t2m error is poleward of 60 degrees, but sea ice - not graph topology - is the obvious candidate there for the same boundary-condition reason.

Caveat: negative skill against persistence is diagnostic of a missing anchor, not proof of one. It is consistent with several causes, including delta-normalisation behaviour over near-constant fields.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: The correction here is a change of METRIC, not a refutation of the earlier bias analysis. Both are true: systematic bias is far more polar-concentrated (~55%) than total squared error (~32% for z500). Bias is the part a structural fix is most likely to remove, so the RMSE share is arguably a pessimistic bound and the bias share an optimistic one. The honest range for what a perfect polar fix could deliver sits between them.

Part of the Antarctic signal is the ERA5 mean-sea-level-pressure-over-ice artifact: MSL is reduced to sea level through roughly 3 km of ice, so some of that error is in the target, not the model. No graph fixes it. The Arctic bands carry no such excuse.

The training loss and this evaluation are both cos(lat)-weighted, so the poles are already down-weighted on both sides. The shares above are AFTER that down-weighting, which is what makes 2.4x over-representation meaningful rather than an artifact of counting grid cells.

Skill vs persistence is a ratio against a baseline that itself varies by zone. A high skill score in the storm track does not mean the absolute error is acceptable there - it means the model beats a weak baseline by a lot, because persistence is very bad where weather moves fast.
Single seed, 51 initial conditions from one year (2018), one checkpoint per model.

ideas.title: Graph reconstruction 1 of 3 - stitch the two pole rows together
ideas.verdict: Proposal: add edges across each pole so that nodes on opposite longitudes of the same pole row become graph neighbours. Assessment: the defect is real and confirmed - 288 pole-row nodes emit 2016 L0 edges and not one of them crosses a pole; the widest longitude gap any pole-row edge spans is 7.5 degrees, where a true over-the-pole link spans about 180. Two nodes at 88.75N on opposite meridians are about 275 km apart in physical space and dozens of hops apart in the graph, so a system crossing the pole is structurally invisible. But the payoff is BOUNDED AND SMALL: everything poleward of 75 degrees is 7.3% of day-10 z500 squared error, so even a perfect fix caps out near 3.7% global RMSE. Do it first anyway, because it is the cheapest change on the list, it is builder-only, it leaves the parameter count untouched, and it is unambiguously falsifiable.

sections.heading: What changes

items: src/graph_builder.py only: for each pole row, connect each node to the node(s) at longitude + 180 degrees (and optionally their immediate neighbours), so information can travel over the pole instead of around it.
No model change. Node count, edge feature dimension and parameter count are unchanged, so this is purely a connectivity edit and existing checkpoints remain shape-compatible.

Today the only polar knob is row_aware_knn.polar_neighbors_from_adjacent_row (currently 2), which forces a couple of links into the adjacent row. Nothing in the current config surface can create a cross-pole edge.
Write it to a NEW graph filename. Overwriting an existing graph path silently changes every run that references it and destroys comparability with the current baselines.

sections.heading: What it can and cannot buy

columns: Share of z500 day-10 squared error
rows: -3.7% if the error there went to zero
-8.5% only if error poleward of 60 were halved

blocks.text: The first row is the honest scope of this change on its own. The second row requires the benefit to propagate equatorward into the 60-75 band, which cross-pole edges alone should not do much for - that band's problem is anisotropy, not the missing pole crossing, and it is idea 2's target. Judge this experiment on polar-band RMSE from scripts/evaluate_zone_rmse_dominance.py, not on global RMSE, which may not move outside noise even if the fix works.

sections.heading: How to test it honestly

items: Train a clean arm from scratch on the new graph rather than warm-starting from a checkpoint fitted to the old one. Weights load across graph versions because they are per-node and per-edge, which is exactly the trap: a warm-started run measures how fast the model unlearns the old topology and is biased toward it.
Use hidden 128 as the workhorse. It is 1.66x cheaper per epoch than hidden 160 and statistically tied with it at day 10, which is the horizon this change targets.

With rollout checkpointing off and the processor compiled, a full h128 arm (100-epoch base plus 27-epoch curriculum) is roughly 4 h rather than the 11.4 h it used to be, so a clean arm is affordable and there is no reason to compromise the comparison.

Primary metric: the 90S-75S and 75N-90N rows of the zone table, against 3.10% and 4.16% for z500 today. Secondary: whether msl polar skill improves, since msl is where the polar signal was first seen.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: The Antarctic half of the polar signal is partly the ERA5 mean-sea-level-pressure-over-ice artifact - the target itself is an extrapolation through about 3 km of ice. No graph change fixes that, so expect the Arctic to respond and the Antarctic to respond less.

The loss is cos(lat)-weighted, so pole rows carry roughly 2% of an equator row's weight. Adding capacity without adding incentive may produce little movement. If cross-pole edges underdeliver, test a reweighting before concluding the topology was not the problem.
A cross-pole edge joins points that are physically close but meteorologically joined only through the polar vortex. It is possible the model learns little from it even with capacity and incentive.
7.3% of the budget means a real success may still be invisible in global headline RMSE. Decide the evaluation metric before running, or the result will be arguable either way.

ideas.title: Graph reconstruction 2 of 3 - azimuth-stratified neighbours from 45 degrees poleward
ideas.verdict: Proposal: stop selecting neighbours by raw distance at high latitude. Instead partition the compass around each node into sectors and take the nearest neighbour in each, so every node keeps a roughly isotropic receptive field regardless of latitude. Assessment: this targets a larger and better-evidenced defect than idea 1. On a lat-lon grid, zonal spacing collapses toward the poles while meridional spacing stays fixed, so distance-ranked k-NN degenerates into a one-dimensional zonal ring: the same-row share of edges climbs from 25% at the equator to 56% at 60-75 degrees and 75% poleward of 75, while meridional reach per hop falls from 208 km to 122 km to 69 km. Crucially this reaches the 60-75 band, which holds 25.1% of day-10 z500 squared error - three and a half times more than the polar caps idea 1 addresses. Still builder-only and still parameter-count neutral. This is the graph change with the best ratio of reach to cost.

sections.heading: The degeneracy, measured (L0 of graph_2p5_k8_l3k24_hybrid_row_aware_L3_v4.pt)

blocks.text: A node at 60-75 degrees spends more than half its message-passing budget talking to nodes at its own latitude, and reaches only 122 km north-south per hop against 208 km at the equator. Whatever number of hops the processor has, the effective north-south receptive field shrinks with latitude. Azimuth stratification fixes that without changing k: it changes WHICH k neighbours are chosen, not how many. row_aware_knn already does a crude version of this by forcing one or two links into the adjacent rows; this generalises it and applies it continuously rather than only at the pole rows.

sections.heading: Why this is the better first real bet

items: Reach: the 60-90 range it fixes carries 32.4% of day-10 z500 squared error and 33.8% of msl, against 7.3% and 8.0% for the polar caps alone.
It is still a graph-builder change with no model edit and no parameter change, so it costs one graph rebuild plus one clean training arm, roughly 4 h at hidden 128 with the speedups applied.

It composes with idea 1 rather than competing: stratification fixes the direction of the receptive field, cross-pole edges fix the topology hole at the very top. Build both into one graph once each is validated separately.
It is the one change that also touches the 45-60 band (41.9% of error) at its edges, where degradation is mild (1.23x) but not zero.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: The 45-60 band holds the most error and is only 1.23x degraded, so most of that 41.9% is probably NOT a graph problem at all - it is the storm track, where the weather is genuinely hardest. Skill vs persistence there is 0.556, among the better scores in the table. Do not expect this change to move the biggest band much.

Forcing isotropy costs something: a stratified neighbour may be considerably further away than the nearest one, so each node's messages carry less local information. There is a real chance of trading fine-scale skill at high latitude for directional coverage, and the mid-latitude bands could get slightly worse.

Choice of sector count is a free parameter with no principled default here. Too few sectors and the degeneracy survives; too many and every node is forced to talk to distant nodes. Expect to sweep it, which multiplies the experiment cost.
Same incentive caveat as idea 1: cos(lat) weighting means the loss barely sees the region this fixes.

The hierarchy inherits the anisotropy at every level and L3 has no nodes poleward of 80 degrees at all. Stratifying L0 alone leaves the coarse levels lat-lon; the coarse-scale polar gap is only closed by idea 3.

ideas.title: Graph reconstruction 3 of 3 - replace the lat-lon processor mesh with an icosahedral or HEALPix mesh
ideas.verdict: Proposal: keep the lat-lon grid for input and output, but run message passing on a quasi-uniform spherical mesh - icosahedral as in GraphCast and Keisler, or HEALPix as in DLWP-HPX - with encoder and decoder mapping between the grid and the mesh. Assessment: this is the only option on the list that removes the anisotropy everywhere rather than patching it at high latitude, and the only one that fixes the coarse levels, where L3 currently has zero nodes poleward of 80 degrees. It is also by far the most expensive and the only one that genuinely breaks warm-starting, because the processor no longer operates on grid nodes. Recommendation: do NOT start here. Ideas 1 and 2 are cheap and they measure how much of the polar gap is topology at all. If they recover most of the polar deficit, this is not worth the rewrite; if they recover little, that is the evidence that justifies it.

sections.heading: What it fixes that the cheaper ideas cannot

items: Uniform resolution at every level. The current hierarchy is four lat-lon coarsenings, so anisotropy is inherited all the way up and the coarsest level (162 nodes) reaches a maximum |lat| of exactly 80.00 degrees with nothing beyond it. Long-range polar information has no coarse path at all.

It removes the pole as a special case entirely: no pole rows, no cross-pole stitching, no sector heuristics. Ideas 1 and 2 are both patches on a coordinate singularity that a uniform mesh simply does not have.
It is what the published systems that beat this class of model actually do, so the approach is not speculative - only its payoff in this codebase is.

sections.heading: What it costs

rows: New grid-to-mesh and mesh-to-grid mapping; both must be written and tested
Genuinely broken - processor weights are tied to a different node set, unlike ideas 1 and 2
Not reusable for the processor; every comparison arm retrains from scratch
Anything that assumes a 72x144 processor node layout needs revisiting
Highest of the three; a large change evaluated against a baseline that is already strong

blocks.text: The 2.7x training speedup makes the retraining affordable - a clean hidden-128 arm is roughly 4 h - so compute is no longer the blocker. Implementation and debugging time is, and so is the risk of comparing a freshly-written mesh path against a well-tuned lat-lon path that has had many iterations of quiet fixes.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: The measured error budget does not obviously demand this. Poleward of 60 degrees is 32.4% of day-10 z500 squared error; the band holding the most error (45-60, 41.9%) sits where the lat-lon graph is only 1.23x degraded and where the model already scores its best skill against persistence. A uniform mesh may deliver much less than its reputation suggests here.

Published icosahedral models differ from this one in many ways at once - training data, parameter count, loss, resolution, rollout schedule - so their success is not attributable to the mesh alone and should not be read as a forecast for this change in isolation.

A new mesh introduces its own artifacts. Icosahedral meshes have twelve pentagonal vertices; HEALPix has its own discontinuities at face boundaries. Trading a known, measured, localised defect for an unfamiliar one is a real risk on a model that currently works.

The interpolation at the encoder and decoder is itself lossy, and at 2.5 degrees the grid is coarse enough that grid-to-mesh interpolation error may be a meaningful fraction of what the mesh is supposed to save.

ideas.title: Training is ~2.7x slower than it needs to be
ideas.verdict: Claim: the 27-epoch hidden-160 curriculum run cost 12.95 h of wall time and roughly 2.7x of that is recoverable without touching the optimisation recipe, because two execution settings are silently wrong. Assessment: the two mechanisms are confirmed by direct reading of the repo's own code, and the speedup by direct benchmark through the repo's Trainer rather than by estimate - before any lever is pulled, the benchmark harness reproduces the production run's logged peak memory (3.49 GB benchmarked against 3.497509 GB logged at S10) and its logged throughput. Rollout-step checkpointing was paying a full extra forward pass for memory nobody needed (3.5 GB peak on a 46 GB card), and torch.compile as previously written compiled nothing at all because the hot path calls model.forward_steps(), which an OptimizedModule does not intercept. Turning both off/on correctly gives 0.8471 -> 0.3926 s per micro-batch on the L40S and 0.5992 -> 0.3125 s on the 97 GB card; a same-seed one-epoch A/B moved train_avg by 1e-6 (bf16 reassociation noise, not behaviour). The honest confounds are real and limit the headline: peak memory goes 3.5 -> 22.1 GB, so the run can no longer share a card; at 1.5 degrees turning checkpointing off is worth only ~1.24x and the compile lever was never measured there at all; the equivalence A/B was run at S=2 only; the whole-curriculum projection is one measured S=10 ratio divided into the logged total, not an observed fast run; and most of the benchmark figures were live session measurements that were never written to a file in this repo, so only the code citations, the epoch_logs.csv numbers and the four rows recorded in the fast config header are independently re-checkable.

sections.heading: Evidence 1 - where the 12.95 h went (27 epochs of runs/dense_l3k24_hidden160_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt_s1_200ep/epoch_logs.csv, summed)

blocks.text: There is nothing to optimise outside the train loop: validation, checkpointing and the dataloader together are 2.45% of wall time. Backward alone is 64.7%, and backward is exactly what rollout-step checkpointing inflates, since checkpointing re-runs the forward of every rollout step during the backward pass. Per-epoch train time is almost perfectly linear in rollout length: train_time(S) = 278.88*S + 11.67 seconds, R^2 = 0.99973 over all 27 epochs. Nine curriculum stages S=2 to S=10 at 3 epochs each means the cost is dominated by the long-rollout tail. All per-stage seconds quoted in this paragraph are the train_time_sec column, the same column the fit uses, not whole-epoch wall time: the three S=10 epochs are 2797.9, 2798.8 and 2798.7 s of train time each, versus a mean of 591 s at S=2 (596.7, 587.7, 589.3). Whole-epoch times including validation are higher - 2840 s at S=10 and 632 s at S=2 - and it is those whole-epoch figures that sum to the 46603 s total above.

sections.heading: Evidence 2 - the benchmark (repo Trainer, S=10, batch 4 x accum 3, 2 repeats per config, uncontended cards, torch.cuda.synchronize around forward and backward)

items: The peak column is L40S throughout, so that the four rows are on one basis. The 97 GB card's own peak for the both-levers row is 22.08 GB, essentially the same figure on a different allocator; the entry quotes 22.1 GB when it needs one number.

Same-card speedups: 1.43x from dropping checkpointing on the L40S, 2.16x with compile on top. On the 97GB card, 1.44x then 1.92x. Cross-card, as-run L40S to fully-optimised 97GB card is 2.71x (0.8471 / 0.3125). That 2.71x is the single value this entry uses for the S=10 both-levers cross-card speedup everywhere it appears.

Harness validation before trusting any of this: the as-run row reproduces the production run's own logged numbers - 3.49 GB benchmarked peak against 3.497509 GB logged at S10, and a benchmarked throughput of 4.607 samples/s against 4.68 logged. The memory check is exact and independently re-checkable against epoch_logs.csv; the throughput check is a session measurement (see the provenance caveat below).
The compile-only row is the memory-constrained fallback: 2.95 GB peak, still ~1.4x faster than as-run, and it fits anywhere the original fitted.

Provenance: the fast config's header comment records the L40S column's 0.8471 / 3.49, 0.5908 / 27.51 and 0.3926 / 22.10, the 97 GB card's 0.3125 / 22.08, and the compile-only fallback's 2.95 GB peak. The 97 GB card's 0.5992 and 0.4150, the compile-only 0.6088 timing, and the 4.607 samples/s validation were live session measurements that were never persisted. They are self-consistent with what is recorded (0.8471 / 0.6088 = 1.39x reproduces the header's '~1.4x'; 0.5992 / 0.3125 = 1.92x), which supports them but does not verify them.

sections.heading: Trap 1 - the two checkpointing config flags are aliases for one mechanism (src/trainer.py, lines 218-219 and 2197-2213)

blocks.text: src/trainer.py reads two independent config flags at lines 218-219, activation_checkpointing and checkpoint_rollout_steps, then gates a single code path on their disjunction at line 2200: not (bool(getattr(self, "activation_checkpointing", False)) or bool(getattr(self, "checkpoint_rollout_steps", False))). Because the test is an OR, setting exactly one of them to false changes nothing - the other keeps the recompute fully on. There is no second, finer-grained mechanism behind the first flag: grepping src/models.py and src/processor.py for checkpoint returns no hits, so there is no intra-model layer checkpointing anywhere. Both flags feed the same two torch.utils.checkpoint call sites in _forward_model_step_train, lines 2208 and 2213, which wrap one whole rollout step with use_reentrant=False.

items: Measured on the L40S, both half-settings: turning off only activation_checkpointing, and turning off only checkpoint_rollout_steps, each reproduced the fully-on peak of 3.50 GB and each showed no speedup. Memory is the comparison that can be made like for like here - all three settings report the same 3.50 GB peak through train.py, against 3.497509 GB logged by the production run - and it is unambiguous: neither half-setting frees a byte. The throughput figures recorded for the half-settings in that session were on a different basis from the per-micro-batch table above and could not be reconciled to it, so they are not published.
Practical consequence: anyone who turned off the flag they remembered and re-benchmarked would have concluded the lever does not work. Both must be false.

The mechanism is correct for what it does - it trades one extra forward per rollout step for activation memory. At S=10 that is ten extra forwards per micro-batch, which is why it shows up as 64.7% backward rather than as a forward cost.

sections.heading: Trap 2 - torch.compile(model) is a silent no-op (src/trainer.py 2165-2187 and 563-594, src/models.py 288 and 301)

blocks.text: torch.compile returns an OptimizedModule that intercepts only __call__ and forward. The training hot path never goes through either: src/trainer.py lines 2165-2187 hold eight call sites, all of the form self.model.forward_steps(previous, current, ...), and forward_steps is a plain method defined at src/models.py line 301, so attribute lookup resolves straight through the wrapper to the uncompiled method. Compiling the top-level model therefore costs compile time and buys exactly zero - and it fails silently, with no warning, because nothing is wrong from PyTorch's point of view.

items: The fix is to compile the submodule that is invoked normally. src/models.py line 288 is h = self.processor(h, diagnostics_collector=diagnostics_collector) - an __call__, so the wrapper does intercept it - and the processor carries the bulk of the compute.
This is now stated in the docstring of _maybe_compile_processor (src/trainer.py 563-571) so the next person does not rediscover it.

Equivalence, one epoch, same seed, compiled vs not: train_avg 0.342493 vs 0.342494; valid_S10_final 1.463244 vs 1.463258. That is bf16 reassociation noise from kernel fusion changing summation order, not a behaviour change. These four numbers are recorded in the fast config's header comment.

sections.heading: Whole-curriculum projection (one measured S=10 ratio divided flat into the run's logged 46603 s total - NOT a stage-by-stage model)

rows: As run (L40S, checkpointing on, no compile)
Both levers, staying on the L40S
Both levers, 97GB card, S10 stage dropped

blocks.text: This is arithmetic on the logged total, not an observed run, and the method is exactly one division. The 97 GB row is 46603.3 s divided by the S=10 per-micro-batch ratio 0.8471 / 0.3125 = 2.71, giving 4.78 h, which the fast config header records as 4.77 h. The L40S row uses the same-card S=10 ratio 0.8471 / 0.3926 = 2.16. The last row takes the as-run total minus the three S=10 epochs (46603.3 - 8520.9 = 38082.4 s = 10.58 h), divides by the same 2.71, and gets 3.90 h, which is 3.32x the as-run 12.95 h.

A correction to an earlier draft of this entry, stated plainly because it weakens the projection: that draft described this section as applying per-stage multipliers measured at S=2, S=5 and S=10 (2.47x, 2.89x, 2.65x) to the run's own per-stage times. It did not - the published figures are the flat division above - and those per-stage multipliers were never written to any file in this repo, so they cannot be re-checked and have been removed rather than re-quoted. The honest consequence is that the projection rests on a single ratio measured at S=10 alone, assumed without measurement to hold at every shorter rollout. That assumption is not load-bearing for the headline, because short stages are a small share of the cost (S=2 and S=3 together are 9.4% of train time), but it is an assumption and not a measurement. The 2.65x that draft attributed to S=10 also disagreed with the 2.71x the fast config records for the same quantity; 2.71x is the value this entry now uses throughout, on the basis stated in Evidence 2.
The last row is a recipe question, not a speed one: dropping the S10 stage is only free if S10 training is not carrying the day-10 skill, which this measurement does not address.

sections.heading: Ruled out - things that look like levers and are not

items: Batch size. The GPU is already compute-saturated at batch 4, and a 10-step rollout is ten sequentially dependent forwards, so adding width does not reduce latency. Measured with checkpointing off on the L40S: batch 6 x accum 2 gave +0.04% over batch 4 x accum 3 - noise. On the 97GB card, batch 12 x accum 1 gave +12% for 81.49 GB peak, roughly 3x the memory for a tenth of the speedup, and it does not fit the L40S at all. Keep batch 4 x accum 3. These three figures are session measurements with no artifact in the repo.
Dataloader. 31.9 s across all 27 epochs, 0.07% of wall time. Nothing to win. This one is straight out of epoch_logs.csv.

fp16 instead of bf16. This is a hardware-spec argument, not something benchmarked here: sm_89 and sm_120 tensor cores run fp16 and bf16 at the same rate, so fp16 would only reintroduce GradScaler overflow risk for no expected gain. Untested in this repo.

Multi-GPU DDP. Not implemented - grepping src/ and scripts/ finds no init_process_group, no DistributedDataParallel wrap, and src/data.py builds a plain DataLoader at line 531 with no DistributedSampler. This is a feature to write, not a setting to flip, and it is worth less than the two levers above until they are on. This one is fully verifiable by grep.

sections.heading: What shipped

items: A compile_processor config flag in src/trainer.py (plus compile_processor_mode). _maybe_compile_processor runs at line 552, deliberately AFTER any checkpoint restore, because compile rewrites the submodule's state_dict keys to processor._orig_mod.* and would not match a stored checkpoint.
_canonical_model_state() (src/trainer.py 596-605) strips the ._orig_mod. prefix on save, so checkpoints written by a compiled run stay loadable by uncompiled runs and by scripts/evaluate.py.
If torch.compile raises, it is caught and the run continues eager - a compile failure must never cost a training run.

It refuses to start alongside EMA: the EMA shadow and backup dicts are keyed by live parameter names, which compile rewrites, and that key mapping is untested. Raise rather than silently write EMA state under mismatched keys.

A drop-in twin config, configs/experiments/config_2p5_l3_hidden160_dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt_s1_200ep_fast.yaml. Diffed against the as-run config it changes only the run and experiment names, three tags, the two checkpointing flags and compile_processor - lr, warmup, cosine, curriculum and effective batch 12 are byte-identical.

sections.heading: Honest caveats

items: Peak memory goes 3.5 GB -> 22.1 GB. The old config could share a GPU with another user's job; this one cannot. That is a real operational cost, not a rounding detail, and on a shared box it may outweigh the speedup. The compile-only fallback (2.95 GB, ~1.4x) exists for exactly that case.

Provenance: most of the benchmark numbers in this entry were live session measurements that were never written to a file in this repo, and a repo-wide grep finds no artifact for them. Independently re-checkable are the code and grep claims, everything drawn from epoch_logs.csv (the Evidence 1 table, the linear fit, the logged 4.68 samples/s and 3.497509 GB), and the four benchmark rows plus the A/B numbers recorded in the fast config's header comment. NOT re-checkable are the 97 GB card's 0.5992 and 0.4150, the compile-only 0.6088, the 4.607 samples/s harness validation, the batch-size sweep figures, and every 1.5-degree number below. Either the benchmark output gets persisted into the repo and cited, or those figures should be read as one operator's session log.

All memory figures are for the 2.5 degree grid. The 1.5 degree grid has 2.8x the nodes (121x240 = 29040 against 72x144 = 10368), so re-measure before enabling anything there. What was measured at 1p5, L3 h128, S10: checkpointing on 7.92 GB / 2.880 samples/s; off at batch 4, 61.69 GB / 3.411 samples/s; off at batch 2 x accum 6, 31.26 GB / 3.567 samples/s. That is ~1.24x, and it is the checkpointing lever ALONE - no compiled-processor measurement was ever taken at 1.5 degrees, so the compile half of this entry is entirely untested there and the combined 2.7x headline must not be quoted for 1.5 degrees in either direction.

The numerical equivalence A/B was run at S=2 only. Longer rollouts compound more arithmetic, so equivalence at S=10 is inferred, not measured. The compile speedup itself has one persisted measurement, at S=10.

Epoch times on this box vary enormously between identically-configured runs because of GPU contention, which is why no absolute hour figure here should be trusted to better than a factor. Verifiable instance: runs/dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt and runs/dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_flat_lr1e7 are both hidden_dim 128, both 2,473,847 parameters, both batch 4 x accum 3, differing only in lr, min_lr and warmup_epochs - and they averaged 383.8 s against 661.6 s per S=2 epoch (1.72x) and 1697.3 s against 4327.0 s per S=10 epoch (2.55x). All benchmark rows in this entry were taken on idle cards back to back, so the same-session ratios are trustworthy; the projected absolute hours are indicative and a real run will land wherever contention puts it.

The projection is one measured S=10 ratio divided into this run's logged total. It is arithmetic on measurements, not an observed end-to-end fast run, and it assumes without measurement that the S=10 ratio holds at shorter rollouts - nobody has yet run the full 27-epoch curriculum with the fast config and timed it. Until someone does, treat 4.77 h as an estimate with the contention caveat above stacked on top of it.

ideas.title: The curriculum ends LR-frozen, not converged - and the last stage is wasted
ideas.verdict: Claim: the 27-epoch S2-to-S10 rollout curriculum stopped improving because its single warmup-cosine LR schedule ran out of step size, not because the rollout objective ran out of signal - and the final S10 stage bought nothing that beat the standing best. Assessment: the LR-freeze reading is well supported through S9, the wasted-last-stage reading is real but single-seed. The best checkpoint is epoch 23 of 27, inside stage S9, and the whole S10 stage (2.37 h, 18.3% of a 12.95 h run) never beat it. The run defines its own noise band - valid_S10_final spans 0.001253 peak-to-peak over epochs 24-27, all at LR below 3e-6 and with no trend - and the stage entries into S6, S7, S8 and S9 all produced drops larger than that band (3.9x, 3.9x, 4.5x and 1.4x it), the last of them at a learning rate of 5.3e-6. The S10 stage entry's apparent -0.001253 drop is numerically identical to the noise band and carries no weight in either direction. Meanwhile train_loss_final fell monotonically inside every stage right through epoch 27 - the optimizer was still descending, the step size was gone. Two confounds bound the conclusion: the size of any gain from an LR restart is extrapolated rather than measured (stage-transition gains conflate new-horizon exposure with learning rate, and S8's own within-stage change was a worsening of +0.39%), and the only flat-LR control that exists is hidden_dim 128 warm-started from a different base, so it is suggestive but not architecturally matched.

sections.heading: Evidence 1 - the best checkpoint is epoch 23 of 27, in stage S9 (training_metrics.csv and epoch_logs.csv, subject run)

blocks.text: Epoch 23 jointly minimises valid_S10 (0.141999) and valid_S10_final (0.261364) and maximises skill_S10 (0.718717, against a constant persistence_S10 of 0.504827). It is the global optimum on all three metrics across all 27 epochs. Epoch 23 is the second of the three S9 epochs (train_rollout_steps = 9 for epochs 22-24). The four epochs that follow - one more at S9 and the entire S10 stage - never match it: the best valid_S10_final in the S10 stage is 0.261741, which is 0.14% worse.

items: Run: runs/dense_l3k24_hidden160_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt_s1_200ep, hidden 160, dense l3k24 v4 graph, 27 epochs, 46603 s total = 12.95 h.
Warm-started from runs/s1only_2p5_l3_hidden160_base_200epoch_dense_l3k24/best_ckpt.tar (best valid_S1 = 0.0174192, at epoch 200).

LR schedule is a single warmup_cosine across the whole run - lr falls monotonically from 5.0e-5 at epoch 1 to 1.0e-6 at epoch 27, with no per-stage restart. The stages are rollout-horizon stages only; nothing about the schedule is aware of them.

sections.heading: Evidence 2 - per-stage best valid_S10_final, and the LR the stage was entered at (training_metrics.csv, 3 epochs per stage)

blocks.text: Every stage from S3 through S9 improved the metric. S10 is the only stage that did not. The improvements shrink monotonically from S5 onward while the LR available to exploit each new horizon shrinks by about a third per stage on average. The successive stage-entry LR ratios are 0.97, 0.91, 0.84, 0.77, 0.69, 0.59, 0.46 and 0.32, a geometric mean of 0.656 - so the decay is mild early and steep late, and only the last two transitions are at or beyond a halving. By S10 the model is being shown a horizon it has never trained on, at 3.4% of the learning rate it had at S2.

sections.heading: Evidence 3 - cost rises monotonically with horizon while gains shrink (epoch_time from training_metrics.csv)

items: Epoch time is almost exactly linear in the rollout horizon: a least-squares fit over stages S2-S10 gives t = 51.7 + 279.1 * S seconds. Each added rollout step costs a fixed 279 s per epoch.
The S10 stage cost 8521 s = 2.37 h, 18.3% of the run, and produced nothing that beat the standing best from epoch 23.
Counting from the best checkpoint: epochs 24-27 cost 11093 s = 3.08 h, 23.8% of the run, and improved nothing. Nearly a quarter of the compute is downstream of the optimum.

sections.heading: Evidence 4 - the central claim: LR-freeze, not convergence (valid_S10_final and train_loss_final per epoch, subject run; every delta below is judged against one explicitly defined noise band)

blocks.text: The noise band is defined once, from this run's own flat tail, and used everywhere in this entry: over epochs 24-27 - all at LR below 3e-6 - valid_S10_final spans 0.261741 to 0.262994, a peak-to-peak spread of 0.001253 (0.48% about a midpoint of 0.26237) with no trend in either direction. Anything smaller than 0.001253 is not a result on this run.

If the curriculum had converged, new horizons would stop helping. Through S9 they did not. The stage entries into S6, S7 and S8 dropped valid_S10_final by 0.004904, 0.004913 and 0.005617 - 3.9x, 3.9x and 4.5x the noise band. The entry into S9 moved it from 0.265669 (epoch 21) to 0.263934 (epoch 22), a drop of 0.001736 or -0.65%, at a learning rate of 5.34e-6: 1.4x the noise band, marginal but outside it. So the horizon signal was still demonstrably live at 5.3e-6, which is where the schedule had already spent 89% of its step size.

The S10 stage entry cannot be used as evidence and is not used here. It moved valid_S10_final from 0.262994 (epoch 24) to 0.261741 (epoch 25) at LR 1.71e-6, a drop of 0.001253 - numerically identical to the noise band, because epoch 24 is the maximum and epoch 25 the minimum of the very window that defines it. The last stage entry that survives the noise floor is S9's.

items: train_loss_final falls monotonically inside all nine stages without exception, including the last: S10 gives 0.21047, 0.20885, 0.20800 across epochs 25-27. The optimizer was still descending on the objective it was given; it simply had no step size left to convert that into validation gain. This, and not the S10 validation wobble, is what carries the LR-freeze reading at the very end of the run.

The S10 stage best (0.261741, epoch 25) never beats the standing best (0.261364, epoch 23). The epoch-24-to-25 move is a recovery inside the flat tail, not a new optimum, and must not be read as a stage gain.
The three S10 epochs run at LR 1.71e-6, 1.18e-6 and 1.00e-6 - the cosine floor. The stage with the largest per-epoch cost in the run (2840 s) is the one given the least ability to learn.

sections.heading: Evidence 5 - valid_S1 degraded 13.5% over the curriculum, and it is not overfitting (s1_overfit_curve.csv)

blocks.text: valid_S1 rose from 0.018186 at epoch 1 to 0.020640 at epoch 27, +13.5%, and is +18.5% against the 0.0174192 of the 200-epoch S1 base it warm-started from. But the train-valid gap widened by only 0.0004157 of the 0.0024540 total, so about 83% of the valid_S1 degradation is a shift in the training loss itself, not a generalisation failure. The model is not memorising - it is being moved. The rollout objective penalises error growth over 10 steps, and that is best served by a smoother, more dissipative one-step operator than pure one-step MSE would select. The one-step skill is being traded away deliberately, and the trade is worth it: skill_S10 goes from 0.634015 at epoch 1 to 0.718717 at epoch 23.

sections.heading: Evidence 6 - diminishing returns, and why extending the curriculum is a bad trade

blocks.text: Fitting the per-stage gain magnitude log-linearly over stages S4 to S9 gives delta(S) = 0.2096 * exp(-0.4634 * S), i.e. each added rollout step buys about 37% less than the last (exp(-0.4634) = 0.629). The fit is restricted to S4-S9 deliberately: S10's delta is positive (+0.000377) and cannot enter a magnitude fit at all, and S2-S3 sit in the warm-start transient. Extrapolating that curve to stages S11 through S20 at 3 epochs each gives a total further gain of about -0.0034 in valid_S10_final - roughly 1.3% relative - for about 36.5 h of compute at the fitted epoch cost. That is 2.8x the entire run so far for a 1.3% metric move, and it is an extrapolation of a curve whose last measured point already violated it.

sections.heading: Recommendation

items: Do not extend the curriculum past S10. The measured marginal gain at S9 is already only -0.003285 for 2.14 h - 2.6x the noise band and falling - and S10 returned nothing that beat the standing best, for 2.37 h.

Spend the compute on a second cosine restart at S9 or S10 instead. Nine epochs at S10 cost about 7.1 h at the fitted 2842.3 s per epoch, which is about a fifth (19.5%) of the 36.5 h that one extra decade of curriculum stages would cost (Evidence 6), and it attacks the constraint that is actually binding. The horizon signal was demonstrably not exhausted at S9 (Evidence 4); the learning rate was.

Practical form: reload runs/dense_l3k24_hidden160_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt_s1_200ep/best_ckpt.tar (epoch 23, S9), pin train_rollout_steps at 10, and run a fresh warmup_cosine from something in the 5e-6 to 1e-5 range - roughly the LR the model had entering S8 (1.16e-5) or S9 (5.34e-6), which is the last part of the schedule where the run was still moving valid_S10_final by more than its own noise band. That range is a starting point chosen from where step size still existed; it is not a projection of what the restart will buy, for the reason given in the second confound below.

Track valid_S1 alongside valid_S10_final during the restart. If the S1 degradation accelerates sharply while valid_S10_final stalls, that would falsify the LR-freeze reading and point at a genuine capacity or objective limit instead.

Cheaper preregistered check first: rerun only the S10 stage (3 epochs, 2.37 h) from the epoch-23 checkpoint at a restarted LR. Precommit to the noise band - it counts as a win only if it beats 0.261364 by more than 0.001253. If it does, the hypothesis holds and the full 9-epoch restart is justified.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: "The S10 stage is wasted" is a single-seed, single-run observation. It rests on a gap of 0.000377 in valid_S10_final between the S9 and S10 stage bests - which is a third of the 0.001253 noise band defined in Evidence 4. On this run's own noise floor the S10 stage is indistinguishable from neutral, not proven harmful; what is solid is that it cost 2.37 h and returned nothing that beat epoch 23. Never training on the evaluation horizon is a real risk that this metric may not capture; before dropping S10 by default, verify a no-S10 variant against valid_S10_final = 0.261364.

The size of the gain from an LR restart is EXTRAPOLATED, not measured. Nothing in this run restarts a learning rate, so there is no direct observation of what one buys. The tempting anchor - the -0.65% drop at the S9 transition - is confounded twice over: it is only 1.4x the noise band, and whatever gain it represents is driven by new-horizon exposure rather than by learning rate. The clean within-stage counter-example is S8: with the horizon held fixed, its own three epochs went 0.264649, 0.264922, 0.265669, a change of +0.39%, i.e. a worsening. Stage-transition gains must not be quoted as evidence for what an LR restart would buy.

A flat-LR sibling run exists (runs/dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_flat_lr5e7, lr and min_lr both pinned at 5.0e-7 over the same S2-to-S10 3-epoch curriculum) and is suggestive, but its config_resolved.yaml shows hidden_dim 128 and init_from_checkpoint pointing at runs/s1only_2p5_l3_hidden128_base_100epoch_dense_l3k24/best_ckpt.tar - a different width warm-started from a different base trained for half as many epochs. It is NOT an architecturally matched control and cannot be used to isolate the LR effect. A proper control is a hidden-160 run from the same 200-epoch base with the schedule as the only change.

The log-linear diminishing-returns fit has 6 points, is fitted on stage bests rather than on repeated measurements, and excludes the one stage (S10) that contradicts it. Its R-squared is not reported here because with 6 points and a hand-chosen window it would overstate confidence. Use the 36.5 h / 1.3% extrapolation as an order-of-magnitude argument against extending the curriculum, not as a forecast.

The noise band itself is estimated from four consecutive epochs of one run, so it is an order-of-magnitude floor rather than a calibrated error bar, and it is measured on the flat tail where the model is barely moving - a restart at higher LR may well have a wider epoch-to-epoch spread. It is used here to reject claims, which is the direction it can support; it should not be used to certify a small gain as real.

valid_S10_final is a single scalar over a fixed validation set. The S10 stage could have improved properties this metric does not see - spectral fidelity at long lead, blow-up rate on rare initial conditions, per-band polar skill - and the entry makes no claim about those. The full-eval artifacts under this run's diagnostics_full_eval and evaluation_test_weekly52 were not opened for this analysis.

ideas.title: hidden 128 vs 160 - tied at day 10, separated at day 1 to 5
ideas.verdict: Claim: widening the processor from hidden 128 to hidden 160 buys a large, unambiguous short-range gain that has almost entirely decayed by day 10. Assessment: the measurement is solid, the mechanism is not. Day-1 RMSE improves 11.6 to 16.0 percent across all six headline variables with non-overlapping 95 percent CIs, day 5 still holds 5.9 to 8.7 percent, and by day 10 all six CI pairs overlap - on five of the six each run's point estimate also falls inside the other run's interval, q700 being the sole exception, where the two point estimates fall just outside each other's intervals but the intervals themselves still overlap. h128 is nominally ahead on day-10 z500 (683.83 vs 687.46 m2/s2), which on this evidence is a tie. Day-10 ACC still favours h160 by +0.012 to +0.050 on all six, but only q700 is significant. The tempting reading, that h128 buys its day-10 RMSE by over-smoothing, is a hypothesis and not a result: the headline h128 run has no variance-ratio diagnostic, and the nearest available h128 proxies actually retain MORE day-10 z500 variance than h160 - though that proxy comparison is itself confounded by learning rate AND by rollout stage, so it does not refute the hypothesis either. Three confounds dominate everything here: the headline pair is not base-matched (h128 warm-started from a 100-epoch S1 base, h160 from a 200-epoch one); the strongest "h128 hits a capacity ceiling" argument leans on an h128 base trained on a 3x sparser L3 graph, so it confounds width with connectivity; and the evaluated checkpoints are not stage-matched (h128 at epoch 27 / S10, both h160 runs at epoch 23 / S9). The most durable finding is elsewhere, but it too must be stated at the right strength: the three day-10 z500 values in the base-versus-width comparison (683.83, 687.46, 701.42) have mutually overlapping CIs, so neither lever is established at day 10. What is not inside the day-10 noise band is the S1 base itself - doubling it from 100 to 200 epochs improved the base's own valid_S1 by 14.6 percent with no architecture change, while +55 percent parameters on a 100-epoch base bought no measurable day-10 gain at all. On that basis: spend compute on the S1 base before spending it on width.

sections.heading: Evidence 1 - day 1: h160 wins on every variable and it is not noise (both runs, evaluation_test_weekly52/S10/evaluation_metrics.csv, 51 initial conditions 2018-01-02 to 2018-12-18, 1000-sample bootstrap 95% CI)

blocks.text: All six intervals are disjoint at day 1, with wide margins - the closest pair (t2m) still leaves a gap of 0.073 K between h160's upper bound and h128's lower bound. At day 5 the ordering is unchanged and the margin has roughly halved: h160 is better by -5.89% (u850), -6.12% (q700), -6.31% (msl), -6.91% (z500), -7.63% (t850) and -8.72% (t2m). Five of the six day-5 intervals are cleanly disjoint; msl is disjoint only by a hair (h160 upper 395.913 Pa vs h128 lower 395.949 Pa, a gap of 0.04 Pa) and should be read as borderline rather than established.

sections.heading: Evidence 2 - day 10: the advantage has fallen into the noise floor (same files, lead_time 10)

blocks.text: All six day-10 CI pairs overlap. On five of the six, each run's point estimate additionally falls inside the other run's 95% CI, in both directions. q700 is the single exception: h128's 1.2316e-3 sits above h160's CI upper bound of 1.2258e-3, and h160's 1.2059e-3 sits below h128's CI lower bound of 1.2135e-3, while the two intervals still share the region 1.2135e-3 to 1.2258e-3. So q700 is the one variable showing a hint of genuine day-10 separation - consistent with Evidence 3, where q700 is also the only variable whose ACC intervals are disjoint.

z500 illustrates the general case. h128 683.83 with CI 661.99 to 704.06 and h160 687.46 with CI 665.07 to 711.58 - the intervals share 39.0 of h128's 42.1 m2/s2 of width, i.e. about 93 percent overlap, and the 3.63 m2/s2 gap between the point estimates is under a tenth of either interval. The h128 win on z500 is a tie, not a win, and the same is true of the h160 wins on t2m, t850, msl and u850. Only the sign pattern (five of six favouring h160) is suggestive, and five of six is not significant on its own.

sections.heading: Evidence 3 - day-10 ACC keeps a lead that RMSE does not show (same files, acc and acc_ci columns, lead_time 10)

blocks.text: h160 is ahead on ACC for all six variables at day 10, by +0.012 to +0.050, and notably it is ahead on z500 (+0.0116) - the one variable where it is nominally behind on RMSE. Only q700 clears the disjoint-CI bar (0.4292 vs 0.4327, a gap of 0.0035). t2m is the largest gain at +0.0500 but its intervals still overlap by 0.009. So the ACC story is a consistent direction on six of six with one significant case, which is stronger than the RMSE picture but is not by itself a proven separation.

sections.heading: Interpretation - the over-smoothing story is a HYPOTHESIS, and the one proxy test available is too confounded to settle it

blocks.text: ACC rewards retained anomaly amplitude while RMSE rewards damping - a model that shrinks toward climatology lowers RMSE and lowers ACC at the same time. h160 being ahead on ACC while tied on RMSE at day 10 is the signature one would expect if h128 were buying part of its day-10 RMSE by over-smoothing. Stated plainly: this was not directly tested. The winning h160 run has diagnostics_full_eval/epoch_0023_variance_ratio.csv; the headline h128 run dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt has NO variance_ratio.csv and no variance_ratio key anywhere in its final_full_diagnostics.json. That gap is real and still open as of this entry.

There is, however, a partial proxy. Two other h128 curricula, dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_flat_lr1e7 and _flat_lr5e7, are computationally identical to the headline h128 run (same hidden_dim 128, same v4/l3k24 graph, same 2,473,847 parameters, same batch size; their config_resolved.yaml differs only in lr, min_lr and warmup_epochs) and they DO carry variance-ratio diagnostics. Comparing them to h160 gives the table below - all on the validation split, but NOT at a matched point in the curriculum. Each run's diagnostic is taken at its own evaluated checkpoint: h160's is epoch 23, its global-best checkpoint, which sits inside the S9 stage (train_rollout_steps 9), while both h128 proxies are at epoch 27, the end of their S10 stage (train_rollout_steps 10). Verified in training_metrics.csv, run_diagnostics.log and fixed10_global_best_metrics.json.

The result is mixed and, on the decisive variable, backwards. On msl the h160 model retains more day-10 variance (0.8348 vs 0.8240 and 0.8127), consistent with the hypothesis. On z500 it retains LESS (0.9614 vs 0.9723 and 0.9748) - meaning the h160 model is the more damped one on exactly the field where h128 nominally wins day-10 RMSE. t2m is effectively a tie near 1.0 for all three.

Two caveats sit on the proxy, and they push the same way. First, learning rate: the flat-LR runs trained at 1e-7 and 5e-7 rather than 5e-5 cosine, so they sit much closer to their initialisation checkpoint than the headline h128 run does, and they are a lower bound on how much the headline run's training moved its variance ratio. Second, and it bites harder, the comparison is not stage-matched: h160's ratios come from an S9-trained checkpoint and the h128 proxies' from S10-trained checkpoints, and S10 is precisely the stage that trains at the horizon being scored. A stage of rollout training at the longest horizon could plausibly change day-10 variance retention on its own, so the z500 reversal cannot be attributed to width. Conclusion: the over-smoothing explanation is NOT supported by the only h128 evidence that exists, but this proxy is too confounded to refute it either. Carry it as an open question, not as the reading of the ACC-vs-RMSE split, and settle it with a direct diagnostic on the headline h128 checkpoint.

sections.heading: Cost - what the extra width actually costs (model_summary.txt and training_metrics.csv in both runs, 27 training epochs each, 3 epochs per stage)

items: Parameters: 2,473,847 (h128) vs 3,844,932 (h160), +55.4%, read from trainable_parameters in each run's model_summary.txt.

Compute cost: mean ratio 1.660x over the nine stage-matched pairs, range 1.609x to 1.685x - a remarkably stable multiplier, and notably ABOVE the 1.554x that the +55.4% parameter growth would predict if cost were parameter-linear. It is not parameter-linear: attention and message passing scale with hidden width differently from parameter count, so the extra width costs somewhat more time than it costs parameters.

Epoch time is almost exactly linear in rollout length. Fitted on the nine per-stage mean epoch times: h128 epoch_time = 46.4 + 164.8*S seconds, h160 = 51.7 + 279.1*S seconds, both R^2 = 0.9997. Refitting on the raw 27 per-epoch times gives the same coefficients with R^2 = 0.9996 (h128) and 0.9997 (h160). The h160 slope is 1.69x the h128 slope while the intercepts differ by only 5.4 s, i.e. the extra width costs per rollout step, not per epoch of setup.

Full-curriculum wall clock: 7.77 h (h128) vs 12.95 h (h160) for 27 training epochs each - but see the wall-clock warning below before using those two numbers for anything, and note that 27 epochs each describes the training, not the evaluated checkpoints, which differ (see confounds).

blocks.text: Raw wall-clock across runs on this box is NOT comparable. Two computationally identical h128 curricula (dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt vs _flat_lr1e7 - same parameters, same graph, differing only in learning rate) recorded mean S2 epoch times of 383.8 s vs 661.6 s (1.72x) and S10 times of 1697.3 s vs 4327.0 s (2.55x). The same pattern shows in the S1 bases: the two h160 base runs are config-identical except for epoch count, yet averaged 319.8 s/epoch (100-epoch run) vs 210.3 s/epoch (200-epoch run), a 1.52x spread, and the 100-epoch run's own per-epoch times range 215.6 s to 328.7 s within a single run. GPU contention, not configuration, explains those. This is exactly why the 1.66x figure is quoted from nine stage-matched pairs inside two runs rather than from total wall clock.

sections.heading: Base epochs versus width - the day-10 RMSE differences here are all within noise (day-10 z500, evaluation_test_weekly52/S10 in all three runs)

blocks.text: Read this table with the same bar the rest of the entry applies: all three 95% CIs mutually overlap, and every one of the three point estimates falls inside both other intervals. 701.42 sits inside h128's 661.99 to 704.06; 687.46 sits inside the h160-100ep run's 680.81 to 721.55. By the day-10 test used in Evidence 2, these three runs are tied on day-10 z500 RMSE, and no claim below rests on their differences.

items: h160 warm-started from a 100-epoch S1 base scored 701.42 m2/s2 at day 10, nominally worse than h128's 683.83 despite +55.4% parameters and 1.66x the training cost. Within noise, per the paragraph above. The honest statement is that width alone bought no measurable day-10 improvement - NOT that it made the day-10 forecast worse.

Holding width fixed at 160 and only doubling the S1 base from 100 to 200 epochs moved day-10 z500 from 701.42 to 687.46 (-2.0%) and day-10 z500 ACC from 0.4715 to 0.5041 (+0.033). The same caveat applies to the RMSE half of that: it is directional, not established. The ACC move is in the same direction as the six-of-six ACC pattern in Evidence 3, which is corroborating but also not individually significant.

The evidence that does not depend on the day-10 bootstrap at all is the base's own validation loss: the h160 100-epoch S1 base finished at valid_S1 0.020386 (train 0.018738), the h160 200-epoch base at valid_S1 0.017419 (train 0.015870) - 14.6% better valid_S1 with no architecture change. Both from training_metrics.csv, both on the v4/l3k24 graph, and the 200-epoch base's best valid_S1 is its final epoch (200), so it was still improving when it stopped. This is a much larger relative move than anything in the day-10 tables and it is measured directly rather than through a 51-IC bootstrap - though it too is single-seed, and it is a one-step metric, so it does not by itself prove a day-10 benefit.

Practical conclusion at the strength the evidence supports: the width lever produced no day-10 gain measurable above noise, while the base-epoch lever is the only one of the two with an effect clearly outside noise anywhere in this comparison (14.6% on the base's own valid_S1). Before buying width, buy S1 base epochs. And the 200-epoch h160 base has not plateaued, so the next increment on that axis is probably not exhausted either.

sections.heading: Honest confounds - this is the part that changes what to run next

items: The headline pair is NOT base-matched. dense_l3k24_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt (h128) is tagged warmstart_from_dense_l3k24_S1_100ep; the winning h160 run is tagged warmstart_from_hidden160_S1_200ep, and the tags match the actual init_from_checkpoint paths in both config_resolved.yaml files. An unknown share of the headline day-1 to day-5 gap is therefore base duration rather than width. The h160-on-a-100-epoch-base row is the closest thing to a base-matched comparison available, and on day-10 z500 it says width alone gains nothing measurable - it does not say width loses, because that difference is inside the CIs.

The evaluated checkpoints are NOT stage-matched either. All three runs trained 27 epochs, but each was evaluated at its own global-best checkpoint, and those do not land at the same point in the curriculum: h128 at epoch 27, the end of its S10 stage (train_rollout_steps 10), and BOTH h160 runs at epoch 23, inside S9 (train_rollout_steps 9). Confirmed from checkpoints.global_best in each run's fixed10_global_best_metrics.json. The h160 numbers therefore come from a model that never finished training at the 10-step horizon it is scored on, while the h128 numbers come from one that did. Whether that helps or hurts h160 at day 10 is untested; it is a real asymmetry in the comparison either way, and it is the same asymmetry that undercuts the variance-ratio proxy above.

CRITICAL, and the reason not to state a capacity result: the strongest available 'h128 hits a ceiling' argument compares h160's 200-epoch base valid_S1 of 0.0174192 against h128's 200-epoch base train loss of 0.018457 (valid_S1 0.020026) - h128 not even fitting the training set as well as h160 fits the validation set. But that h128 base is runs/s1only_2p5_l3_hidden128_base_200epoch_overfit_probe, and its config_resolved.yaml specifies graph_2p5_k8_hybrid_row_aware_L3_v3.pt with graph_format_version 3 and l3_k_neighbors 8, while every other run in this comparison uses graph_2p5_k8_l3k24_hybrid_row_aware_L3_v4.pt with graph_format_version 4 and l3_k_neighbors 24 - a 3x denser L3. Verified by opening both files. That comparison therefore confounds width with L3 connectivity and must NOT be reported as a clean capacity result.

Consequence for the next experiment: warm-starting an h128 curriculum from that v3 base would initialise a v4/l3k24 curriculum from weights fitted to a different L3 neighbourhood. The parameter count matches exactly (both 2,473,847) so the checkpoint would load without error - which makes this an easy mistake to make silently - but it is not a like-for-like test and its result would be uninterpretable. A clean answer needs an h128 200-epoch base retrained on v4 first.

Cost of that clean test: at the measured v4 h128 rate of 130.8 s/epoch (from s1only_2p5_l3_hidden128_base_100epoch_dense_l3k24, 3.63 h for 100 epochs), a 200-epoch v4 h128 base is about 7.3 h of GPU time; the v3 200-epoch base actually took 15.37 h at 276.6 s/epoch on a contended box. Budget roughly 7 to 15 h for the base, on top of about 8 h for the 27-epoch h128 curriculum.

The over-smoothing hypothesis remains untested for the headline h128 run - no variance_ratio.csv exists for it - and the flat-LR h128 proxies that do exist point against it on z500 while being confounded by both learning rate and rollout stage (see Interpretation). Do not cite it as a finding in either direction.

All test metrics are single-seed, from 51 initial conditions in a single year (2018-01-02 to 2018-12-18), with bootstrap CIs from 1000 resamples at the 95% level (bootstrap_seed 42). The CIs are per-run and not paired across runs, so disjoint-interval tests here are conservative for day 1 to 5 but say nothing reassuring about day 10. Sub-percent differences at day 10 are ties, full stop - and that rule is applied in this entry to the base-versus-width table too, not only to the headline pair.

sections.heading: What to run next (ranked by information per GPU-hour)

items: 1. Cheapest and highest value: emit a variance-ratio diagnostic for the existing h128 headline checkpoint. No training required, it is an evaluation-side diagnostic, and it directly settles whether the ACC-vs-RMSE split at day 10 is a damping artifact. The flat-LR proxies hint the answer may be no for z500, but they are confounded by learning rate and by rollout stage, which is exactly why the direct measurement is worth having. Emit it at the h160 stage too, or compare like for like at epoch 27.

2. Train an h128 200-epoch S1 base on the v4/l3k24 graph (about 7 to 15 h). This is the only way to get a base-matched h128 vs h160 comparison and to turn the capacity-ceiling argument from confounded into clean. Everything else in this entry is downstream of it.

3. Then run the h128 curriculum from that base (about 8 h) and re-evaluate. If h128-from-200ep closes the day-1 gap, the width advantage was largely base duration; if it does not, width is real at short lead and simply does not survive to day 10.

4. Independently, extend the h160 S1 base past 200 epochs - its best valid_S1 is its final epoch, so that curve had not flattened. Base epochs are the only lever in this entry with an effect clearly outside noise (14.6% on valid_S1), which makes this the better-odds bet on the current architecture.

5. Do not spend compute on hidden 192 or beyond until 2 to 4 report back. On present evidence the day-10 return on width is not measurable above the noise floor, and the day-1 return, while large and solidly significant, is confounded with base duration until item 2 lands.
