ideas.title: At 1.5 degrees the curriculum model beats the KAI reference at day 10 and loses the short leads
ideas.verdict: Claim: the 1.5 degree L3 h128 curriculum model (runs/dense_l3k24_1p5_curriculum_S2toS10_3ep_initckpt, epoch 27, 2.47M params) beats the KAI 1.5 reference. Assessment: true at day 10, false at the short leads, and the headline is misleading without a lead qualifier - but there is no single crossover day. On 51 weekly 2020 initial conditions the model wins day-10 RMSE on all six headline variables (u850 -17.2%, msl -14.5%, q700 -13.8%, z500 -13.4%, t850 -10.1%, t2m -5.7%) and wins day-10 ACC on only four - t850 (0.415 vs 0.423) and t2m (0.411 vs 0.418) go the other way. The per-lead curves are the actual finding, and the crossover is variable-dependent, spanning more than three days: by linear interpolation of the RMSE difference it is u850 5.88, q700 6.39, msl 6.80, z500 7.36, t850 7.77, t2m 8.90. In whole leads the model first wins u850 at day 6, msl and q700 at day 7, z500 and t850 at day 8, and t2m not until day 9. On z500 KAI is 2.30x better at day 1 (52.5 vs 121.0), and averaged over leads 1-10 KAI is still ahead on every one of the six variables, by +6.8% on z500 and by +19.5% on t2m. This is the same short-lead-for-long-lead trade the rollout curriculum produces at 2.5 degrees, where valid_S1 degrades and valid_S10 improves over the same 27 epochs; the crossover is that trade made visible on a test set. Anyone who needs day 1-3 skill should not use this checkpoint. Main confound: the two evaluations are not verified to share a protocol - experiments/kai_1.5.csv carries no metadata whatsoever beyond lead time and channel index, so protocol agreement is assumed and unverified.

sections.heading: Evidence 1 - day 10, model vs KAI 1.5 (51 weekly 2020 initial conditions; fixed10_global_best_metrics.json vs experiments/kai_1.5.csv)

blocks.text: Six RMSE wins, four ACC wins. The two ACC losses are the two temperature fields, and they are small (0.008 and 0.007 absolute); the RMSE wins on the same two fields are the smallest of the six (-10.1% and -5.7%). Ranked by day-10 RMSE win the order is u850 -17.2%, msl -14.5%, q700 -13.8%, z500 -13.4%, t850 -10.1%, t2m -5.7%. So the day-10 advantage is largest on wind, pressure and humidity and smallest on temperature - but note that q700 outranks z500, so this is not a clean dynamic-versus-thermodynamic split and should not be described as one. The model's own bootstrap 95% CI on day-10 z500 RMSE is 673.5 to 711.4 (1000 resamples, seed 42), so the KAI value of 799.4 sits well outside it - but that interval is over our 51 initial conditions only and is not a paired test against KAI. Both beat persistence at day 10 (z500 persistence 1088.9, msl 952.3, u850 7.284).

sections.heading: Evidence 2 - the shape of the result: z500 RMSE by lead, and where the curves cross (same two sources)

blocks.text: The z500 crossover falls between day 7 and day 8 - day 7.36 by linear interpolation of the RMSE difference. That figure is z500-only and must not be quoted as a global switch point; the per-variable table below spans more than three days. The gap is not a small early offset: at day 1 the model's z500 error is 2.30x KAI's, and the model needs until day 8 to close a deficit it starts with. What the model actually has is a flatter error growth curve. Over leads 1 to 10 the model's z500 RMSE grows 5.7x (121.0 to 692.1) while KAI's grows 15.2x (52.5 to 799.4). That is the signature of rollout training: the model is optimised so that errors compound slowly, at the price of a worse single-step map.

columns: First whole lead the model wins RMSE

blocks.text: There is no single switch point. The spread is 5.88 to 8.90 days, just over three days wide, and it orders the same way the lead-averaged result does: the variables the model recovers earliest (u850, q700) are the ones where it loses least on the lead average, and t2m, which it does not win until day 9, is the worst lead-average loss. Any statement of the form 'the model wins after day N' is only true of one variable at a time.

sections.heading: Evidence 3 - averaged over leads 1-10 KAI wins every variable (model column verbatim from fixed10_global_best_summary.csv rmse_avg_1_10; KAI column is the mean of the ten CSV rows)

blocks.text: This is the honest summary line and it goes the other way from the day-10 table: on a lead-averaged basis KAI is ahead on all six variables, not just z500. The variable ordering is largely preserved between the two views while the sign flips - the fields where the model gains most at day 10 are the fields where it loses least on the lead average. Day-10 win magnitude descending: u850 17.2, msl 14.5, q700 13.8, z500 13.4, t850 10.1, t2m 5.7. Lead-average loss magnitude ascending: u850 0.7, q700 3.3, msl 5.3, z500 6.8, t850 14.5, t2m 19.5. The correspondence is close but not exact: msl and q700 swap places between the two lists. The endpoints are the clear cases - u850, with the largest day-10 win (-17.2%), is nearly a tie on average (+0.7%), while t2m, with the smallest day-10 win (-5.7%), is the worst lead-average loss (+19.5%). So 'we beat KAI at 1.5 degrees' is a statement about long lead only, and any claim stated without a lead qualifier is wrong.

sections.heading: Evidence 4 - the same trade is visible in training, at both resolutions (valid_S1 and valid_S10 columns of training_metrics.csv)

items: At 2.5 degrees, over the 27 curriculum epochs, valid_S10 improves from 0.21087 to 0.15204 (-27.9%) while valid_S1 degrades from the S1 base run's best value of 0.023362 to 0.026847 (+14.9%).
At 1.5 degrees the same pattern, same magnitudes: valid_S10 0.21910 to 0.15364 (-29.9%), valid_S1 from the S1 base best 0.026896 to 0.030812 (+14.6%).

Both valid_S1 figures are referenced to the S1 base run's best value, and the basis changes the number materially. Referenced instead to the curriculum's own epoch-1 valid_S1 the same degradation is +10.2% at 2.5 degrees (0.0243606 to 0.026847) and +9.1% at 1.5 degrees (0.0282502 to 0.030812). Every valid_S1 degradation percentage in this entry is base-best-referenced; state the baseline whenever the number is quoted, because the two conventions differ by about five percentage points. The base bests are both at epoch 100.

The mechanism is therefore not a 1.5 degree artefact. The curriculum trades single-step accuracy for rollout stability by construction, at both resolutions, by a consistent 14-15% on valid_S1 against the base best. The 1.5 degree crossover against KAI is just the first time that trade has been made visible against an external reference rather than against our own validation loss.

sections.heading: Cost - the 1.5 degree L3 h128 pipeline has run 38.6 h, about 3.4x the matched 2.5 degree runs (epoch_time and peak_gpu_memory columns of training_metrics.csv; node and edge counts from node_counts, edge_counts and grid_shape in each run's config_resolved.yaml)

blocks.text: The GB label on peak GPU memory is not an assumption: src/trainer.py line 4160 populates the peak_gpu_memory column from cuda_peak_allocated_gb, so the stored values 7.9188 and 2.8815 are gigabytes by construction. Memory scales at 2.75x, close to the L0 node-count ratio of 2.80x, which is what a pure activation-size argument predicts. Wall clock scales at 3.38x, and every problem-size proxy lands near 2.81x rather than 3.38x: total nodes across the four graph levels are 38,700 vs 13,770 (2.810x) and total edges 317,280 vs 112,752 (2.814x). So there is a real gap of roughly 20% between how much bigger the problem is and how much longer it takes, and it is currently unexplained.

HYPOTHESIS, not a measurement: the gap is data loading and lower GPU utilisation at the larger grid. Nothing in this entry tests that. training_metrics.csv records only epoch_time and peak_gpu_memory per epoch - there is no I/O timing, no profiler trace and no utilisation sampling in any file cited here, and competing explanations (kernel efficiency at the larger tensor shapes, memory-bandwidth limits, host-side graph handling, or contention from other jobs on the box) have not been ruled out. If the gap did turn out to be recoverable overhead, the arithmetic ceiling would be about 20% of 38.57 h, i.e. roughly 7 h - but that figure is conditional on a diagnosis nobody has made, and it should not be quoted as an available saving. What is measured and safe to use is the ratio itself: budget about 3.4x the 2.5 degree cost for any 1.5 degree experiment.

sections.heading: Tooling - what the two scripts do as they currently stand (scripts/plot_experiment_rmse_acc.py, scripts/run_1p5_eval_maps_comparison.sh)

items: experiments/kai_1.5.csv is a raw per-channel evaluation dump with columns lead_time,variable_idx,original_channel_idx,variable_name,rmse,acc - 737 data rows, 67 channels x 11 leads (0-10). The file is 738 lines including the header, which is the easy way to get the row count wrong. experiments/kai_2.5.csv is a curated 4-column file, variable,timestep,rmse,acc, 10 rows per variable starting at lead 1.

scripts/plot_experiment_rmse_acc.py handles both layouts. _read_kai_csv sniffs the header set, accepting either variable/timestep or lead_time/variable_name, and raises with an explicit message naming both expected column sets if it matches neither (lines 214-222). Both layouts normalise to (variable, timestep, rmse, acc).

It drops the raw layout's lead-0 identity rows (line 235). Precisely: all 67 lead-0 rows have rmse 0.0, and acc is 1.0 for 65 of the 67 - the exceptions are tisr (channel 62) at 0.9999952 and orog (channel 64) at 0.0, so 'rmse 0.0, acc 1.0' is a good description of the rows but not a literal one. Dropping them matters for more than tidiness: leaving them in would both drag every curve to the origin and make the baseline's lead grid 0-10 disagree with the model evaluations' 1-10, which _validate_leads rejects outright (line 295).

keep_variables narrows the 67-channel dump to the six headline variables so the per-channel dump does not flood the plots, and the narrowing is guarded by a non-empty check (lines 237-242) so it only applies when the baseline actually covers a requested variable - otherwise the full set is kept and the gap is reported by _select_variables rather than silently swallowed.

scripts/run_1p5_eval_maps_comparison.sh (271 lines) runs the four stages a 1.5 degree model needs end to end: climatology build, 10-day test rollout evaluation, bias maps, and the KAI comparison overlay. Stage-selectable via STAGES, with DRY_RUN and MODEL=all.

Scope note on this whole section: it describes the current source only. git is not usable in this environment (it reports 'fatal: not a git repository' even with the sandbox disabled, although .git/ exists), so the prior state of either script could not be checked, and this entry makes no claim about what they did or did not support before. Anyone wanting the before-and-after framing should cite the commit.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: Protocol agreement is assumed and unverified, and this is the weakest link in the whole entry. What is known about our side: 51 initial conditions from the 2020 test split at stride 7 (52 requested, 51 selected), first 2020-01-02, last 2020-12-17, calendar-aware, climatology data/stats/kai_1p5_train_dayofyear_climatology.nc built day-of-year from the train split, bootstrap 1000 samples at 0.95 with seed 42. What is known about KAI's side: nothing. experiments/kai_1.5.csv has no header comment, no sidecar file, and no mention anywhere in the repo's markdown; experiments/README_requested_models.md documents kai 2p5 only. Its initial conditions, test year, and climatology are all unknown. If KAI used a different climatology the ACC comparison is invalid; if it used a different or larger IC set the RMSE comparison is noisier than the CIs suggest.

The ACC conventions do appear to match between our evaluation and kai_1.5.csv - both start near 0.99 at day 1 (model z500 0.98866, KAI 0.99778) and decay to about 0.5 at day 10 (0.522 vs 0.472). That is weak but real evidence the climatologies are compatible. It is not proof.

Trap for anyone reading the existing 2.5 degree figures: experiments/kai_2.5.csv uses a completely different ACC convention. Its day-1 z500 ACC is 0.78, decaying to 0.34 at day 10, against 0.998 to 0.472 for kai_1.5.csv on the same variable. A model curve starting at 0.99 overlaid on a baseline curve starting at 0.78 will look like a huge win that is purely a definitional artefact. Its RMSE values are also rounded to 2-3 significant figures (75, 110, 175, 265, ...). ACC overlays against kai_2.5.csv are not directly comparable and should not be read as skill differences.

Single seed, single test year (2020), single checkpoint. No seed-repeat exists for either the 1.5 degree base or the curriculum run, so none of the margins here have a run-to-run error bar - only a within-run bootstrap over initial conditions.
The 51 initial conditions are weekly and therefore serially correlated through the seasonal cycle; the bootstrap resamples them as if independent, which will make the CIs somewhat too narrow.

The crossover days are interpolated from ten discrete leads, not measured at sub-daily resolution, and they carry no uncertainty interval - no bootstrap was run on the crossover itself. Near the crossing the two curves are within a few percent of each other, so the interpolated days are point estimates on noisy differences and the ordering of adjacent variables (q700 6.39 vs msl 6.80, z500 7.36 vs t850 7.77) should not be over-read. The wide separation between the extremes, u850 at 5.88 and t2m at 8.90, is the robust part.

The evaluation JSON records no unit metadata for any variable - the per-variable metric blocks carry only name, variable_idx, channel, rmse and acc. The model and KAI numbers are compared as stored, on matching channel indices (z500 is channel 6 on both sides, and q700 20, t850 33, u850 45, t2m 60, msl 65 all match), so the ratios are meaningful even though the absolute units are undocumented.

The two sides are not matched on parameter count, training data, or compute. KAI's architecture and training budget are unknown, so nothing here attributes the difference to the curriculum rather than to capacity or data.

The 20% excess in the wall-clock ratio over the node and edge ratios is an observation with no diagnosis attached. It is listed in the Cost section as a hypothesis about I/O and utilisation, and it should be treated as an open question, not as a known implementation defect with a known fix.

sections.heading: What to do with this

items: Do not ship this checkpoint for day 1-3 forecasts. Serve the S1 base checkpoint from runs/s1only_1p5_l3_hidden128_base_100epoch_dense_l3k24 for short leads and the curriculum checkpoint at long leads; both checkpoints already exist. There is no single switch day - the per-variable crossovers span 5.88 (u850) to 8.90 (t2m) - so the switch has to be set per variable, or, if one global switch is required for all six, at day 9, which is the first whole lead at which the curriculum checkpoint leads on every variable.

Get the KAI protocol before quoting these margins externally. A single sentence documenting kai_1.5.csv's initial conditions and climatology would convert the strongest caveat in this entry into a verified comparison. Until then, state the assumption whenever the numbers are used.

Test whether the trade is a hyperparameter rather than a law: a lower LR or fewer epochs in the S2-S10 phase should move the crossovers earlier without giving up the day-10 win. The 14-15% valid_S1 degradation is consistent enough across both resolutions to be worth treating as a tunable dial rather than an inevitability - though that consistency is two runs, not a demonstration that the dial turns.

Add a lead-averaged and a short-lead metric to the tracked set. Day-10 RMSE alone selected a checkpoint that loses the lead average on all six variables; a scoreboard that shows only day 10 will keep making that selection.

Profile the 1.5 degree training loop before the next 1.5 degree run. Wall clock scales at 3.38x while nodes and edges scale at 2.81x, and nothing in the current logs explains the difference. One profiling run would establish whether the gap is I/O, utilisation, kernel efficiency or contention - which is the prerequisite for claiming any of it is recoverable. Do not budget the roughly 7 h implied by the gap until that measurement exists.

ideas.title: Polar MSL error is largely a graph-structure problem
ideas.verdict: Hypothesis: most of the MSL error concentrates at the poles because the lat-lon k-NN graph is structurally weak there. Assessment: very likely a major contributor. The polar receptive field per message-passing hop is provably ~6.7x smaller than at the equator and almost purely zonal, there are no cross-pole edges, and the error pattern matches — including over the Arctic, where MSL is a real (non-extrapolated) quantity. Two confounds explain part of the Antarctic signal: the ERA5 MSL-over-ice artifact and the cos(lat) loss downweighting.

sections.heading: Evidence 1 — where the MSL error sits (prev-best run, year-mean bias, area-weighted)

blocks.text: By day 10, ~55% of the global area-weighted squared MSL bias sits poleward of 60 deg on 13% of the Earth (~4x over-represented at each pole). The zonal profile is elevated across the whole cap (~200–270 Pa poleward of 76 deg vs ~33 Pa in the tropics), not just at the last grid row. The Arctic blow-up matters most: Arctic MSL is real (ocean at sea level), so it cannot be blamed on the ERA5 reduction artifact. z500 shows the same southern-cap concentration (~3–4x); t2m much less (~2x) — dynamic fields that need horizontal transport suffer most, pointing at message passing rather than surface physics.

sections.heading: Evidence 2 — the graph is crippled at the poles (graph_2p5_k8_l3k24_hybrid_row_aware_L3_v4.pt, L0, k=8)

items: A polar node gathers information from a ~6.7x smaller physical footprint per hop; k-NN by distance on a lat-lon grid degenerates to a 1-D zonal ring near the poles (zonal spacing ~10 km vs 278 km meridional). row_aware_knn (2 forced adjacent-row neighbors) softens but cannot fix this.

Zero cross-pole edges (0/1008 at both pole rows): nodes at 88.75N on opposite longitudes are ~275 km apart across the pole but dozens of hops apart in the graph. A polar low crossing the pole is structurally invisible.

The hierarchy inherits the anisotropy (L1–L3 are lat-lon coarsenings; polar mean edge stays ~1.4x shorter than average at every level) and L3 has no nodes poleward of 80 deg — the caps lose coarse coverage.
Diagnostics agree: L0 spectral gap lambda_2 = 0.00064 (very slow mixing).

Compounding: the training loss is pure cos(lat)-weighted MSE (src/losses.py LatitudeWeightedMSE), so pole rows get ~2% of an equator row's weight — standard practice (GraphCast does the same), but it means weak incentive on top of weak capacity.

sections.heading: Honest confounds

items: Antarctic MSL in ERA5 is partly an extrapolation artifact (pressure reduced to sea level through ~3 km of ice); every model shows large 'errors' there and no graph will fix that part. The Arctic signal is the clean smoking gun.
Polar MSL variability (annular modes) is naturally high, so some error concentration is expected even with a perfect graph.
Attribution estimate: Arctic blow-up mostly graph; Antarctic roughly half graph, half artifact + downweighting.

sections.heading: Fix plan (ranked)

items: 1. Quick graph rebuild (days, edge-only, weight-compatible with existing checkpoints): (a) azimuth-stratified neighbor selection — nearest neighbor per compass sector instead of 8 nearest, making the receptive footprint isotropic at every latitude; (b) cross-pole stitching for rows poleward of ~85 deg (edges to antipodal-longitude nodes, or a virtual pole supernode connected to the top rings); (c) extend L3 nodes into the polar caps.

2. Structural fix (1–2 weeks): quasi-uniform spherical mesh processor, GraphCast-style icosahedral multimesh (or HEALPix / H3). Keep L0 lat-lon grid for encode/decode; replace L1–L3 lat-lon coarsenings with icosphere refinements. Node budgets line up: icosahedron levels have 162/642/2562 nodes and the current L3 already has 162.

3. Non-graph complement (hours): mask or downweight the msl loss over high orography (orog > ~1500 m) using the existing loss_channel_weighting infrastructure; sp is predicted anyway and is well-defined everywhere.
4. Measurement: add per-latitude-band RMSE to the evaluation so polar skill becomes a tracked metric — global RMSE barely moves even if the caps improve 2x (they are only 13% of the area).

Suggested sequence: do 1 + 3, warm-start from the current best S1 checkpoint, and A/B the polar-band RMSE. If the Arctic error drops substantially, that confirms the mechanism and justifies the icosahedral processor as the durable fix.
